## System of equations in Matrix Form
Consider the following system of equations:
$$
\begin{cases}
2x_1 + 3x_2 + 10x_3 = 5 \\
4x_1 + x_2 + 12x_3 = 6 \\
7x_1 + 2x_2 + x_3 = 10
\end{cases}
$$

::: {.callout-warning title="Exercises" icon="false"}
- How can we write this system in matrix form?
- Solve it using Python.
:::
---

## Matrix Operations using Python

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1-2|3-7|8-10|11-13|14-15|16"
import numpy as np

#Define matrix A and vector b
A = np.array([[2, 3, 10],
                 [4 , 1, 12],
                 [7 , 2, 1]])
b = np.array([5 , 6, 10])

#Inverse A
A_inverse = np.linalg.inv(A)

x = np.dot(A_inverse, b)
print('Solution: ', x)
```

---

## Matrix Operations using R

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# Define matrix A and vector b
A <- matrix(c(2, 3, 10,
              4, 1, 12,
              7, 2, 1),
            nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE)

b <- c(5, 6, 10)

# Inverse A
A_inverse <- solve(A)
x <- A_inverse %*% b

# Solve Ax = b
x <- solve(A, b)
print(x)
```

## Derivatives of a vector

::: {.callout-note title="Gradient with respect to a vector" appearance="default" icon="false"}
- In single-variable calculus:

    $\frac{d}{dx} f(x)$ is the slope of a scalar function of one variable.

- In multivariable calculus:

    If $f(z_1, z_2)$, we can group the variables into a vector:

    $$ z = \begin{bmatrix} z_1 \\ z_2 \end{bmatrix} $$

  then the derivative with respect to a vector is the **gradient**:

    $$
    \nabla_z f(z) =
    \begin{bmatrix}
    \frac{\partial f}{\partial z_1} \\[6pt]
    \frac{\partial f}{\partial z_2}
    \end{bmatrix}
    $$

👉 Take the partial derivative with respect to each coordinate, then stack them in a column vector.
:::

---

Consider:
$$
a = \begin{bmatrix}
a_1 \\
a_2
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
z = \begin{bmatrix}
z_1 \\
z_2
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
B = \begin{bmatrix}
b_{11} & b_{12} \\
b_{21} & b_{22}
\end{bmatrix}
$$

::: {.callout-warning title="Exercises" icon=false}
Verify, by showing all the relevant steps, that:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(i) & \quad \frac{\partial z'a}{\partial a} = z \\[6pt]
(ii) & \quad \frac{\partial a'z}{\partial z} = a \\[6pt]
(iii)& \quad \frac{\partial z'B z}{\partial z} = 2Bz \quad \text{since B is symmetric}
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

## Histograms & Kernel Density Estimation {.section-divider-centered background-color="#0396A6"}

---

## Density Estimation - Introduction
Given some observations from some variable $X$, we would like to obtain an estimate of its density.

::: columns

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.callout-note title="*Parametric vs Nonparametric*" icon="false"}
- **Parametric**: choose a density family (normal, exponential, uniform...) and estimate its parameters from data.

<span style="color:#F28627">*Problem: what if $X$ doesn't follow that family?*</span>

- **Nonparametric** (histograms, KDE) estimates the distribution without strong assumptions.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

np.random.seed(3)

# 1. Generar datos con asimetría positiva
data = np.random.gamma(shape=1.2, scale=2.0, size=500)

# Grilla estrictamente positiva para ambos gráficos
xs = np.linspace(0, data.max(), 300)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4.2), sharey=True)

# --- PANEL IZQUIERDO: Paramétrico (Normal) ---
mu, sigma = data.mean(), data.std()
norm_pdf = stats.norm.pdf(xs, mu, sigma)

axes[0].hist(data, bins=20, density=True, color="gray", alpha=0.5, edgecolor="white")
axes[0].plot(xs, norm_pdf, color="#F28627", linewidth=3, label="Normal fit")
axes[0].set_title("Parametric (Normal)")
axes[0].set_xlabel("X")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Density")
axes[0].legend(loc="upper right")

# --- PANEL DERECHO: No Paramétrico (KDE con corrección de borde en 0) ---
# Se duplican los datos reflejándolos en 0 para corregir el desborde (boundary bias)
data_reflected = np.concatenate([-data, data])
kde_reflected = stats.gaussian_kde(data_reflected)
kde_pdf = 2 * kde_reflected(xs)  # Se multiplica por 2 para conservar el área = 1

axes[1].hist(data, bins=20, density=True, color="gray", alpha=0.5, edgecolor="white")
axes[1].plot(xs, kde_pdf, color="#008080", linewidth=3, label="KDE")
axes[1].set_title("Nonparametric (KDE)")
axes[1].set_xlabel("X")
axes[1].legend(loc="upper right")

# Formato final
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlim(0, data.max())
    ax.set_ylim(0, None)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

:::

## Histogram
> **Key idea:** A histogram is a graphical tool to visualize the distribution of a dataset.

::: columns

::: column


- A **nonparametric method** to estimate the probability density function (PDF)
- Groups data into **intervals (bins)**
- Plots the **frequency** of data points in each bin

:::

::: column
```{python}
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import numpy as np

# Example data
np.random.seed(42)
x = np.random.normal(0, 1, 500)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6,5))
sns.histplot(x, bins=15, color=bse_style.TEAL, edgecolor='black', stat='density', ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel('X')
ax.set_ylabel('Density')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

```
:::
:::

---

## Concept of Density

Let's differentiate between frequency histograms and density histograms, using a dataset with 12 observations: `[2, 3, 5, 5, 6, 8, 8, 8, 10, 12, 15, 17]`

<div class="step-indicator"><span class="step active">1</span><span class="step-line"></span><span class="step">2</span><span class="step-line"></span><span class="step">3</span><span class="step-label">Binwidth</span></div>

::: {.column width="100%"}
### If we fix the number of bins ex-ante, we must derive the binwidth:

<div class="eq-box-wrap"><div class="eq-box" style="padding: 8px 18px; font-size: 0.75em;">

$$
n_{bins} = 3 \;\Longrightarrow\; \text{binwidth} = h = \frac{\max(x) - \min(x)}{n_{bins}} = \frac{17 - 2}{3} = 5
$$

</div></div>

```{python}
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from collections import Counter

data = [2, 3, 5, 5, 6, 8, 8, 8, 10, 12, 15, 17]
bin_edges = [2, 7, 12, 17]
bin_labels = ["Bin 1", "Bin 2", "Bin 3"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 2.15))
counts = Counter(data)
max_stack = max(counts.values())

for val, c in counts.items():
    for i in range(c):
        ax.scatter(val, i + 1, s=150, color=bse_style.TEAL, edgecolor="white", zorder=3)

for edge in bin_edges:
    ax.axvline(edge, color=bse_style.ORANGE, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.3, zorder=2, ymin=0.1, ymax=0.85)

# min / max labels
ax.annotate("min = 2", xy=(2, max_stack + 0.6), ha="center", fontsize=11,
            color=bse_style.PURPLE, fontweight="bold")
ax.annotate("max = 17", xy=(17, max_stack + 0.6), ha="center", fontsize=11,
            color=bse_style.PURPLE, fontweight="bold")

# underbrace-style bracket + label under each bin
brace_y = -0.75
tick = 0.15
for i in range(3):
    x1, x2 = bin_edges[i], bin_edges[i + 1]
    ax.plot([x1, x2], [brace_y, brace_y], color=bse_style.TEAL, lw=2, zorder=1)
    ax.plot([x1, x1], [brace_y - tick, brace_y + tick], color=bse_style.TEAL, lw=2)
    ax.plot([x2, x2], [brace_y - tick, brace_y + tick], color=bse_style.TEAL, lw=2)
    ax.text((x1 + x2) / 2, brace_y - 0.45, bin_labels[i], ha="center", fontsize=10,
            color=bse_style.TEAL, fontweight="bold")

ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xticks(bin_edges)
ax.set_xticklabels([str(e) for e in bin_edges], color=bse_style.ORANGE, fontweight="bold", fontsize=10)
ax.set_xlabel("X")
ax.set_ylim(brace_y - 1.1, max_stack + 1.1)
ax.set_xlim(0, 19)
for spine in ["left", "top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

---

## Concept of Density

<div class="step-indicator"><span class="step">1</span><span class="step-line"></span><span class="step active">2</span><span class="step-line"></span><span class="step">3</span><span class="step-label">Bin limits</span></div>

::: columns

::: {.column width="40%"}
| Bins         | Frequency  |
|--------------|------------|
| [2-7)        | 5          |
| [7-12)       | 4          |
| [12-17]      | 3          |
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

bins_labels = ["[2-7)", "[7-12)", "[12-17]"]
freq = [5, 4, 3]
colors = [bse_style.TEAL, bse_style.PURPLE, bse_style.ORANGE]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3.8))
ax.bar(bins_labels, freq, color=colors, edgecolor="black")
ax.set_ylabel("Frequency")
ax.set_xlabel("Bins")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

:::

---

## Concept of Density

<div class="step-indicator"><span class="step">1</span><span class="step-line"></span><span class="step">2</span><span class="step-line"></span><span class="step active">3</span><span class="step-label">Density</span></div>

::: columns

::: {.column width="48%"}
| Bins         | Frequency  | Width | Density |
|--------------|------------|-------|---------|
| [2-7)        | 5          | 5     | $5 / (12*5) = 0.0833$ |
| [7-12)       | 4          | 5     | $4 / (12*5) = 0.0667$ |
| [12-17]      | 3          | 5     | $3 / (12*5) = 0.05$ |

::: {.fragment}
Mathematically, for bin width $h$ and number of observations $n$:

<div class="eq-box-wrap"><div class="eq-box">

$$ \hat{f(x)} = \frac{1}{nh} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{1}\{x_i \in \text{bin}(x)\} $$

</div></div>
:::
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

bins_labels = ["[2-7)", "[7-12)", "[12-17]"]
density = [5 / (12 * 5), 4 / (12 * 5), 3 / (12 * 5)]
colors = [bse_style.TEAL, bse_style.PURPLE, bse_style.ORANGE]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3.8))
ax.bar(bins_labels, density, color=colors, edgecolor="black")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
ax.set_xlabel("Bins")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

:::

---

## Density ≠ Probability

::: {.callout-warning title="Exam question" icon=false}
*Could the range of values of the vertical axis in a histogram be greater than 1? Justify your answer.*
:::

::: columns

::: {.column width="42%"}
Imagine the following data, **narrower range** (0.10 to 0.35):

`[0.10, 0.15, 0.15, 0.20, 0.20, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.30, 0.35]`

We set 5 bins ($h = 0.25/5 = 0.05$), usual estimator:

<div class="eq-box-wrap"><div class="eq-box" style="padding: 4px 12px; font-size: 0.52em;">

$$\hat f(x) = \frac{1}{nh}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{1}\{x_i \in \text{bin}(x)\}, \; nh = 0.5$$

</div></div>

:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

data = [0.10, 0.15, 0.15, 0.20, 0.20, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.30, 0.35]
n = len(data)
edges = [0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, 0.35]
h = 0.05

labels, densities = [], []
for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
    freq = sum(1 for d in data if (lo <= d < hi) or (hi == edges[-1] and d == hi))
    labels.append(f"[{lo:.2f}-{hi:.2f}{']' if hi == edges[-1] else ')'}")
    densities.append(freq / (n * h))

colors = [bse_style.TEAL, bse_style.PURPLE, bse_style.ORANGE, bse_style.TEAL_LIGHT, bse_style.PURPLE]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.4))
ax.bar(labels, densities, color=colors, edgecolor="black")

ax.axhline(1, color=bse_style.ORANGE, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5)
ax.text(-0.45, 1.25, "height = 1", color=bse_style.ORANGE, fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")

for i, d in enumerate(densities):
    ax.text(i, d + 0.2, f"{d:.0f}", ha="center", fontsize=11, color=bse_style.BLACK, fontweight="bold")

ax.set_xlabel("")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

:::

### Coding Example in R
Important parameters: <code>bins</code>, <code>aes(y = ..stat..)</code>, <code>binwidth</code>, <code>xlim()</code>
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(ggplot2)
library(readr)

tips <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mwaskom/seaborn-data/master/tips.csv")
x <- tips$total_bill

bins <- c(15, 30, 70)
for (bin in bins) {
  p <- ggplot(data = data.frame(x = x), aes(x = x)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = ..density..), bins = bin, color = "black", fill = "skyblue")
  print(p)
}
```

## Kernel Density Estimation

> **Key idea:** Smooth, nonparametric estimate of the probability density function

::: columns

::: column

- Instead of counting frequencies in bins, KDE places a smooth kernel function (usually Gaussian) centered at each data point, and then averages them.

::: {.callout-warning title="The limitation KDE fixes" icon=false}
A histogram is **discrete**: it jumps abruptly at every bin edge. KDE is **continuous by construction** — no bins, no edges, just a smooth curve.
:::

:::

::: column
```{python}
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import numpy as np

# Example data
np.random.seed(42)
x = np.random.normal(0, 1, 500)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6,5))
sns.histplot(x, bins=15, color=bse_style.TEAL, edgecolor='black', stat='density', kde=True, ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel('X')
ax.set_ylabel('Density')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

```
:::
:::

---

## The Kernel Function

<div class="eq-box-wrap"><div class="eq-box" style="padding: 6px 18px; font-size: 0.8em;">

$$\hat{f}_h(x) = \frac{1}{nh} \sum_{i=1}^n K\left(\frac{x - x_i}{h}\right)$$

</div></div>

::: columns

::: {.column width="40%"}
- $n$ is the number of observations
- $h$ is the bandwidth (controls how much each observation's influence spreads)
- $K$ is the **kernel** — any symmetric function integrating to 1. Gaussian is the most common choice, but not the only one:
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

u = np.linspace(-2, 2, 400)

gaussian = (1 / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)) * np.exp(-u**2 / 2)
epanechnikov = np.where(np.abs(u) <= 1, 0.75 * (1 - u**2), 0)
triangular = np.where(np.abs(u) <= 1, 1 - np.abs(u), 0)
uniform = np.where(np.abs(u) <= 1, 0.5, 0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.0))
ax.plot(u, gaussian, color=bse_style.TEAL, linewidth=2.5, label="Gaussian")
ax.plot(u, epanechnikov, color=bse_style.PURPLE, linewidth=2.5, label="Epanechnikov")
ax.plot(u, triangular, color=bse_style.ORANGE, linewidth=2.5, label="Triangular")
ax.plot(u, uniform, color="#888888", linewidth=2.5, label="Uniform (box)")

ax.set_xlabel(r"$u = (x - x_i)/h$")
ax.set_ylabel("K(u)")
ax.legend(fontsize=10, frameon=False)
for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

:::

```{python}
#| eval: true
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# Load data
x = sns.load_dataset("tips")["total_bill"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.3))

# Different bandwidths (smaller → more wiggly, larger → smoother)
tags = ["too wiggly", "reasonable", "oversmoothed"]
for color, bw, tag in zip([bse_style.TEAL, bse_style.PURPLE, bse_style.ORANGE], [0.3, 2, 10], tags):
    sns.kdeplot(x, bw_adjust=bw, label=f"h = {bw}  ({tag})", color=color, fill=True, ax=ax)

ax.set_xlabel("Total Bill")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
ax.legend(fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

```

:::

- **Small $h$**: very wiggly estimate (low bias, high variance).
- **Large $h$**: oversmoothed estimate (high bias, low variance).
- Same bias-variance trade-off as the **binwidth** $h$ in a histogram — just for a smooth curve instead of bars.

---

### Coding example in R

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)

tips <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mwaskom/seaborn-data/master/tips.csv")
x <- tips$total_bill

for (bw in c(0.3, 1, 2)) {
  print(ggplot(data.frame(x = x), aes(x = x)) +
          geom_density(adjust = bw, color = "blue") +
          ggtitle(paste("Bandwidth =", bw)))
}
```

## What is LaTeX (and why use it)?

::: columns

::: {.column width="52%"}
LaTeX is a **typesetting system**, not a word processor: you write plain-text markup, and it *compiles* into a professional PDF — like code, but for documents.

::: {.callout-tip title="Why for assignments" icon=false}
- Clean, consistent math notation
- Regression tables & figures exported **directly** from Python/Stata — no manual formatting
- The same source always reproduces the same PDF
:::


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
<div class="doc-scroll"><img src="../theme/assets/latex-template-full.png"></div>
:::

:::

## Key Commands: Structuring a Document {.smaller}

::: columns

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{.tex}
\section{Introduction}
This is the introduction to the assignment.

\subsection{Motivation}
Here we explain why this analysis matters.

\subsection{Data}
We describe the dataset used.

\section{Results}
We now present our findings.
```

- `\section{}` numbers top-level headings; `\subsection{}` nests one level in
- Numbering, spacing, and the table of contents update **automatically**
- No manual "1.2" typing, no forgetting to renumber after edits
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
<img src="../theme/assets/latex-sections-render.png" class="doc-preview">
:::

:::

---

## Key Commands: Math Notation {.smaller}

::: columns

::: {.column width="48%"}
```{.tex}
\begin{equation}
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i
\end{equation}

Matrices use the bmatrix environment:
\[
X =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & x_{11} & x_{12} \\
1 & x_{21} & x_{22} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
1 & x_{n1} & x_{n2}
\end{bmatrix}, \ \beta =
\begin{bmatrix}
\beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \\ \beta_2
\end{bmatrix}
\]

\[
\hat{\beta} = (X'X)^{-1} X'Y
\]
```

- `equation` numbers the line; `\[...\]` (or `$...$`) doesn't
- rows separated by `\\`, entries by `&`
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
<img src="../theme/assets/latex-math-render.png" class="doc-preview">
:::

:::

## From Python to a Rendered Table {.smaller}

::: {.columns style="align-items:flex-start;"}

::: {.column width="45%"}
```{.python}
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from stargazer.stargazer import Stargazer

m1 = smf.ols("tip ~ total_bill", tips).fit()
m2 = smf.ols("tip ~ total_bill + size", tips).fit()

sg = Stargazer([m1, m2])
sg.rename_covariates({"total_bill": "Total Bill", "size": "Party Size"})

with open("regression.tex", "w") as f:
    f.write(sg.render_latex())
```
Then in LaTex you just call the .tex file 

```{.tex}
\input{regression.tex}
```
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
<img src="../theme/assets/latex-table-render.png" class="doc-preview" style="max-height:420px;">

## A Wilder Option: Tectonic + GitHub in VS Code

::: {.columns style="align-items:flex-start;"}

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-note title="Why bother?" icon=false}
Overleaf's free tier caps you at 2 editors. Git doesn't cap anything — and you get real **pull requests, diffs, and code review** on your `.tex` source, the same workflow you already use for code.
:::

Compile straight from the terminal, as many times as you want, in seconds:

> <code>tectonic main.tex</code>
